issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court exercising certiorari jurisdiction cannot reweigh a tribunal’s factual finding unless the finding involves a reviewable error of law or jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Collector found, after considering oral and documentary evidence, that the land had been cultivated by the tenant’s father and that the recorded difference in his parentage was a clerical error.
The reviewing courts found that the Collector’s finding was supported by evidence and was not based on legally inadmissible evidence or a refusal to admit admissible evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right not to interfere with the finding in certiorari jurisdiction, and there was no justification for setting aside the administrative orders on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, certiorari is supervisory, not appellate: factual findings reached on appreciation of evidence cannot be reopened merely because they may be erroneous. Interference is available where a tribunal acts on legally inadmissible evidence, refuses admissible evidence, makes a finding unsupported by any evidence, exceeds or refuses jurisdiction, or acts illegally or improperly in a way that causes grave miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan.

rule.if: certiorari_review_of_tribunal_finding and finding_based_on_some_evidence and not finding_based_on_legally_inadmissible_evidence and not admissible_evidence_refused and not jurisdictional_or_procedural_illegality_causing_grave_injustice

predicates.certiorari_review_of_tribunal_finding: A party asks a reviewing court to use certiorari to examine a factual finding made by an inferior tribunal.
predicates.finding_based_on_some_evidence: The tribunal’s factual finding is supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.finding_based_on_legally_inadmissible_ev: The tribunal relied on evidence that the law did not permit it to consider.
predicates.admissible_evidence_refused: The tribunal refused to admit evidence that it was legally required to consider.
predicates.jurisdictional_or_procedural_illegality_: The tribunal exceeded or refused its jurisdiction, or acted illegally or improperly in a way that caused grave injustice.

issues.definition: When a certiorari challenge concerns a tribunal finding supported by evidence and none of the stated reviewable errors is present, the rule yields no interference in certiorari.

issues.legal_issue: Land occupied by a tenant at the relevant reference point is assigned to the tenant’s permissible area rather than included in the landowner’s surplus area.
material_facts: The landowner’s surplus area was being determined under the applicable land-tenure scheme.

The Collector found that the tenant’s father occupied the disputed land as a tenant at the relevant reference point, relying on oral and documentary evidence and treating a conflicting entry as a clerical error.
The Collector excluded the disputed land from the landowner’s surplus area and treated it as part of the tenant’s permissible area.
issues.conclusion: The Collector’s treatment of the disputed land as part of the tenant’s permissible area, excluded from the landowner’s surplus area, did not involve an error of law or jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under the scheme of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, the Collector fixes the permissible areas of the landowner and the tenant separately as at the relevant reference point. The Court concluded that the land was properly placed in the tenant’s permissible area on the supported factual finding that the tenant’s father occupied it as a tenant then.

predicates.surplus_area_determination: An authority is determining a landowner’s surplus area and a tenant’s permissible area under a land-tenure scheme.
predicates.tenant_occupied_land_at_reference_point: The tenant or the tenant’s predecessor occupied the land as a tenant at the scheme’s relevant reference point.
predicates.finding_of_tenancy_supported_by_evidence: The authority’s finding that the land was occupied by a tenant is supported by evidence.

issues.definition: When a supported finding in a surplus-area determination establishes tenant occupation at the reference point, the land is excluded from the landowner’s surplus area and placed in the tenant’s permissible area.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative order that refers to irrelevant grounds may stand if relevant, existing grounds independently support the decision and the irrelevant grounds would not have affected its outcome.
material_facts: The Commissioner initially misunderstood the appellants’ position and referred to matters that were not relevant to the real dispute.
Reading the Commissioner’s order as a whole, the Court found that he addressed the tenancy issue and concurred with the Collector’s finding.
The Financial Commissioner considered the evidence and affirmed the finding, and the Court concluded that the Commissioner’s deficiencies had not prejudiced the decision on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The Commissioner’s initial misconception and references to irrelevant matters did not invalidate the administrative decision because they had not prejudiced the outcome.
issues.legal_principle: Where an order refers to multiple grounds, some relevant and existing and others irrelevant or nonexistent, it may be sustained if the authority would have made the order on the relevant grounds and excluding the irrelevant grounds could not have affected the ultimate decision. The Court relied on State of Maharashtra v. B.K. Takkamore and State of Orissa v. Bidyabhushan Mahapatra.

predicates.administrative_order_review: A court is reviewing an administrative order challenged as defective in its reasoning.
predicates.order_contains_relevant_and_irrelevant_g: The order refers to both grounds relevant to the dispute and grounds that are irrelevant or nonexistent.
predicates.relevant_existing_grounds_support_decisi: The relevant, existing grounds are sufficient to support the authority’s decision.
predicates.excluding_irrelevant_grounds_would_not_c: Removing the irrelevant or nonexistent grounds would not affect the decision’s outcome.

issues.definition: When an administrative order includes irrelevant grounds but its relevant grounds independently support the same outcome, the rule yields that the order is sustained.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s objection that evidence was received behind its back does not invalidate an administrative decision when the evidence was received in the party’s presence, the party could challenge it, the challenged document was not relied on, and no prejudice resulted.
material_facts: The appellants alleged that a document was supplied and the Patwari was examined after the matter had been reserved, without their participation.
The Court found no reference to the document in the Collector’s order and concluded that the Patwari was examined in the presence of the parties or their counsel and could be cross-examined.
The Court found that the late examination of the Patwari had not prejudiced the appellants or another party.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of procedurally unfair evidence-taking was not tenable and did not justify interference with the Collector’s order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the asserted irregularity had occurred and whether it prejudiced the affected party; it found that the disputed document was not relied on, the witness was examined in the parties’ presence and was subject to cross-examination, and no prejudice resulted.

rule.if: administrative_order_challenged_for_evidence_procedure and evidence_received_in_party_presence and party_allowed_to_testify_against_evidence and challenged_document_not_relied_on and no_prejudice_from_procedure

predicates.administrative_order_challenged_for_evid: A party challenges an administrative order on the ground that evidence was received through an unfair procedure.
predicates.evidence_received_in_party_presence: The evidence was received while the affected party or its representative was present.
predicates.party_allowed_to_testify_against_evidenc: The affected party was able to challenge the evidence, including by cross-examining the witness where applicable.
predicates.challenged_document_not_relied_on: The decision-maker did not rely on the document alleged to have been received unfairly.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_procedure: The procedure did not cause prejudice to the affected party.

issues.definition: When the evidence procedure was participatory, the challenged document was not relied on, and no prejudice resulted, the rule yields that the procedural objection does not invalidate the order.
